sections.h2: What should a Washington home seller know about the state's housing market?
sections.html:
Washington had an estimated 8,001,020 residents on July 1, 2025, according to the U.S. Census Bureau, living in about 3.44 million housing units. The Census Bureau puts the owner-occupied housing rate at 63.8 percent for 2020 to 2024, and the median value of an owner-occupied home at $564,600 over the same period.

Median gross rent in that period was $1,760 and the median household income was $98,141. These are statewide figures, so check county-level numbers before pricing a particular house.

That is why selling a Washington house starts with the county. The county assessor values your property, the county treasurer collects the tax and records the excise tax paperwork, the county auditor records the deed, and the superior court in your county handles probate and eviction cases. The sections below cover what every Washington seller meets, whatever the town.

sections.h2: How do Washington's 39 counties differ for sellers?
sections.html:
Washington has 39 counties, and population is very uneven. King County, home to Seattle, had 2,344,939 residents in the 2025 Census estimate, almost 30 percent of the state. Garfield County had 2,416. Land area runs from about 174 square miles in San Juan County to 5,268 in Okanogan County.

Counties differ in how they are governed as well. Most use the default commission form, but King, Clallam, Whatcom, Snohomish, Pierce, San Juan and Clark have adopted home-rule charters. Sub-county government is only by incorporated cities and towns, so houses outside city limits deal with the county alone for permits and zoning.

  • Largest: King (2,344,939), Pierce (946,288) and Snohomish (870,656) hold the largest populations.
  • Next tier: Spokane (558,344), Yakima (259,185) and Benton (221,722).
  • Other large counties: Clark (532,119), Thurston (304,261), Kitsap (283,374) and Whatcom (236,392).
  • Smallest: Garfield (2,416), Columbia (4,141), Wahkiakum (4,873) and Ferry (7,517).

sections.h2: How is property tax assessed and collected in Washington?
sections.html:
Counties do the work. The Department of Revenue oversees property tax at the state and local level but does not collect it. County assessors appraise property at 100 percent of true and fair market value, and county treasurers collect the tax and distribute it to local governments. Property tax is the main funding source for public schools, fire protection, libraries and parks.

If you disagree with the assessed value, the appeal goes to the county board of equalization in the county where the property sits. Homeowners who meet age, income or disability criteria may qualify for an exemption or deferral, which the assessor's office explains.

Late payment is expensive. After April 30, unpaid tax is delinquent and accrues 1 percent interest per month, with a 3 percent penalty if it is still unpaid on June 1. If you pay the first half by April 30 but miss the second half due October 31, the unpaid portion accrues 1 percent monthly interest and an additional 8 percent penalty applies to anything still owing on December 1. Ask the county treasurer for a payoff figure before closing so any unpaid balance comes out of the sale proceeds.

sections.h2: Who pays the real estate excise tax when a Washington house sells?
sections.html:
Usually the seller. The Department of Revenue says all sales of Washington real property are subject to the real estate excise tax unless an exemption applies, the seller normally pays, and the buyer becomes responsible if the seller does not. Unpaid tax can create a lien on the property.

The state portion is graduated, and the local portion is added on top. For sales beginning January 1, 2027, the state rates are 1.1 percent on the part of the price up to $551,000, 1.28 percent from $551,000 to $1,551,000, 2.75 percent from $1,551,000 to $3,051,000 and 3.0 percent above that. Agricultural land and timberland use a flat 1.28 percent state rate. Because the thresholds reset every four years, ask the county treasurer which schedule covers your closing date.

The tax is due to the county treasurer on the date of sale, which is the date the deed is notarized, whenever it is recorded. Penalty and interest apply if it is not paid within one month. Inheritance transfers are exempt, but a later sale by the heir is taxable on the full price.

sections.h2: Does Washington tax capital gains or estates when a house changes hands?
sections.html:
Real estate is exempt from the state capital gains tax. That tax, created by RCW 82.87, is 7 percent on the sale of long-term capital assets such as stocks and bonds, applies only to individuals, and lists real estate among its exemptions. Federal tax rules still apply to a home sale, so ask a tax professional about your own gain.

The state estate tax is separate. A Washington estate tax return is required when the gross value of the decedent's property exceeds the filing threshold, which is $3,000,000 for deaths on or after July 1, 2026. The return and any tax are due nine months after the date of death, and interest accrues on unpaid tax even if an extension to file is granted. Families who inherit a house in a larger estate should ask the estate's attorney about this deadline before listing the property.

sections.h2: What Washington laws matter most for inherited, tenant-occupied or creditor-pressured houses?
sections.html:
Three bodies of state law come up again and again for sellers in difficult situations. Each has its own statute chapter, and each is easier to handle with a county-level starting point.

  • Probate: Title 11 RCW. A small estate affidavit under RCW 11.62.010 is limited to $100,000 and waits forty days after death, and a personal representative with nonintervention powers may sell real property without a court order under RCW 11.68.090.
  • Landlord and tenant: chapter 59.18 RCW. An owner who elects to sell a single-family residence must give at least 90 days' written notice to end a tenancy for that cause, and a rent increase needs 90 days' notice.
  • Homestead: chapter 6.13 RCW. The creditor-protection amount is the greater of $125,000 or the county median single-family sale price from the prior calendar year.

Each of these has more detail in the statewide guides on this site. Start with the one that matches your situation, then check the county where the house sits.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in Washington?
faqs.a: The county treasurer. The county assessor sets the value, and the Department of Revenue oversees the system but does not collect the tax. Pay the treasurer in the county where the property is located.

faqs.q: How many counties does Washington have?
faqs.a: Thirty-nine. King County is the largest at 2,344,939 residents in the 2025 Census estimate, and Garfield County is the smallest at 2,416.

faqs.q: Is there capital gains tax on selling a house in Washington?
faqs.a: Washington's capital gains excise tax does not apply to real estate, which is one of its listed exemptions. Federal tax rules are separate, so ask a tax professional about your own sale.

faqs.q: When is the Washington real estate excise tax due?
faqs.a: On the date of sale, paid to the county treasurer. The date of sale is the date the deed is notarized, and penalty and interest apply if the tax is not paid within one month.

faqs.q: Can I appeal my Washington property assessment?
faqs.a: Yes. You may appeal to the county board of equalization in the county where the property is located. Ask the county assessor's office about the deadline and the forms.
